title: How a neuron learns
blurb: Sort pets, draw a line, then watch a real neuron tune itself — round by round — until it beats you.
objectives: What a neuron really is — a line that splits things into two groups
What its two knobs (weights & bias) actually do
How it fixes its own line by learning from mistakes, one round at a time
How to tell if it really LEARNED — or just memorized
Why one neuron isn't enough, and where networks come from

glossary.def: The tiniest part of an AI brain. From two clues it makes one call — by drawing a line.
The line a neuron draws. One side is one group, the other side is the other.
The dials that tilt the line — how much each clue matters.
The dial that slides the line up or down without tilting it — the tipping point.
How many it got wrong. Learning means making the error smaller.
One pass where the neuron checks its mistakes and nudges its dials a little.
Repeating rounds — check mistakes, nudge, repeat — until it's good.
Doing well on NEW examples it never studied. That's real learning, not memorizing.
Many neurons wired together, so their straight lines combine into curves.

steps.title: Part 1 · A robot that sorts pets
steps.body:
Meet a robot with one job: look at a pet and say **cat or dog**. It can't see fur or hear barks — it only gets two clues: **ear size** and **tail length**.

That's it. From two numbers, it has to decide. Sounds hard? You're about to do it yourself first.

steps.title: You be the AI
steps.body: Here are some pets, each with its two clues shown as bars. Sort every one into **Cat** or **Dog**. Trust the clues!
steps.youWillDo: sort the pets yourself, using the clues

steps.title: A quick guess
steps.prompt: If we put every pet on a chart — ear size across, tail length up — do you think **one straight line** could keep most cats on one side and dogs on the other?
choices: Yes, one straight line could split most of them
No, you'd need a curvy line
steps.afterPick: Hold that thought — you'll draw the line yourself next. →

steps.title: Draw the line
steps.body: Drag the two purple dots to swing the line until cats and dogs are on different sides. Get **wrong** as low as you can, then **Lock in**.
steps.youWillDo: drag the line to split cats from dogs

steps.title: So close — but not perfect
steps.body:
You probably got *most* of them, but a few stubborn dots stayed on the wrong side. The groups overlap a little, and a line placed **by hand** can only do so much.

So how could the robot do better than your best try? That's the whole rest of this lesson. First, let's look *inside* the line.

steps.title: Part 2 · What's inside the line
steps.body:
That line isn't magic — it's run by just **two kinds of dial**:

- **Weights** — how much each clue *matters*. They **tilt** the line.
- **Bias** — the **tipping point**. It **slides** the line up or down.

Let's grab the dials and feel what each one does.

steps.title: Which dial?
steps.prompt: You want to make the line **tilt** to a new angle. Which dial should you turn?
steps.afterPick: Let's test it on a real neuron. →
steps.youWillDo: predict which dial tilts the line

steps.title: Turn the dials
steps.body: This is the inside of a neuron. The two clues go in, get multiplied by the **weights**, plus a **bias**, and the total decides the answer. Drag the dials and watch the answer flip — and the math change live.
steps.youWillDo: drag the weight & bias dials and watch the output flip

steps.title: Check yourself
steps.question: Which dial slides the line up or down **without** tilting it?
steps.explain: Right — the **bias** is the tipping point. It moves the line without changing its angle. Weights change the angle.

steps.title: Part 3 · Counting mistakes
steps.body:
To get *better*, the neuron first needs to know how *wrong* it is. So it counts: how many pets are on the wrong side of the line right now? That count is called the **error**.

Learning has one goal: make the error smaller.

steps.title: Guess the shape
steps.prompt: Each round, the neuron nudges its line a little toward the dots it got wrong. If it keeps doing that, what happens to the number of mistakes?
steps.afterPick: Let's watch it as a chart. →
steps.youWillDo: predict what the mistakes will do

steps.title: Watch the mistakes fall
steps.body: Press **Train a round** (or **Auto**). Each bar is how many mistakes the neuron still makes after that round. Watch the bars shrink.
steps.youWillDo: train rounds and watch the mistake bars drop

steps.title: Say it your way
steps.prompt: In your own words, what does **error** mean for the neuron — and what does it want to do with it?
steps.placeholder: Error is… and the neuron tries to…

recall.question: What is the neuron's goal each round?
choices: Keep the error exactly the same
recall.explain: Yes — every round it nudges toward making fewer mistakes. Smaller error = better.

steps.title: Part 4 · One nudge at a time
steps.body:
Here's the trick that makes it all work. The neuron doesn't guess once — it **repeats a round**: look at the mistakes, nudge the dials a tiny bit, check again. Over and over.

Let's do it one round at a time so you can see each nudge.

steps.title: Run it one round at a time
steps.body: Press **Run one round**. Each press, the neuron looks at its mistakes and nudges the line a little. Watch the **wrong** count drop, press by press.
steps.youWillDo: press Run one round and watch each nudge

steps.title: It has real names now
steps.body:
What you just did has names — and now they'll stick:

- The line is the **decision boundary**.
- The dials that move it are the **weights** (and bias).
- **Learning** = nudging those dials a little after each mistake, round after round.

That's the whole secret. Now watch it run full speed.

steps.title: Same thing, sped up
steps.body: Press **Watch it learn**. It starts from a bad line on purpose, then runs the same rounds automatically — wrong dots flash, the line tunes itself.
steps.youWillDo: watch the neuron tune its own line fast

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: When the neuron "learns," what is actually changing each round?
steps.explain: The dots never change — the **dials** do. Moving the weights and bias is exactly what learning is.

steps.title: Part 5 · Did it really learn — or memorize?
steps.body:
Here's a sneaky question. The neuron got great at the pets it practiced on. But did it learn the *idea* of cat-vs-dog… or did it just memorize those exact pets?

There's one way to find out: show it **brand-new pets it has never seen**.

steps.title: Your call
steps.prompt: The neuron aced the pets it studied. How will it do on totally new pets it never trained on?
choices: Just as well — it learned the idea
steps.afterPick: Let's actually test it. The new pets are the hollow dots. →
steps.youWillDo: predict how it does on new pets

steps.title: The real test
steps.body: The **hollow** dots are new pets — the neuron never sees them while training. Press **Train on the studied pets**, then check its score on the new ones.
steps.youWillDo: train, then check the NEW (hollow) pets

steps.title: That's called generalizing
steps.body:
It did well on pets it had **never seen**. That means it didn't memorize — it learned the real pattern. Doing well on new examples is called **generalizing**, and it's the whole point of learning.

(If it had aced the studied pets but flopped on new ones, that's **memorizing** — and it's a trap real AI engineers watch out for.)

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.prompt: Why do we test the neuron on **new** pets instead of the ones it already practiced on?
steps.placeholder: Because if we only tested the practice ones…

recall.question: A neuron scores 100% on its practice pets but only 55% on new ones. What happened?
recall.explain: Exactly — acing practice but failing new ones means it memorized, not learned. Real learning shows up on new examples.

steps.youWillDo: explain why we test on new examples

steps.title: Part 6 · Train one yourself
steps.body: You've seen every piece: clues in, a line, dials, rounds, and the real test. Time to put it together and train a neuron **from scratch**, with no hints.

steps.title: Your neuron
steps.body: New pets, no hints. Set a rough line with the dots, then press **Train my neuron** and watch it finish the job on its own.
steps.youWillDo: set a line, then train your own neuron

steps.title: The whole loop
steps.question: Put it together — how does a neuron learn?
choices: Guess → count mistakes → nudge the dials → repeat
It asks a human for the answer each time
It picks the dials randomly and hopes
steps.explain: That loop — guess, check, nudge, repeat — is the heartbeat of every AI, from this tiny neuron to the biggest models.

steps.title: Part 7 · Some shapes one line can't cut
steps.body:
One neuron draws **one straight line**. That's perfect for two tidy groups — but the world isn't always tidy.

What if one group is *wrapped around* the other, like a ring around its center? Let's see if a straight line can handle that.

steps.title: Can it be done?
steps.prompt: Can a single **straight line** separate a ring of dots from the cluster in its center?
choices: No — a straight line can't wrap around
Only if you tilt it a lot
steps.afterPick: Let the neuron try as hard as it can. →
steps.youWillDo: predict if one line can split a ring

steps.title: Let it try the ring
steps.body: Now the dots make a **ring** around a core. Press **Let it try** and watch — no matter how the neuron tilts its line, it gets stuck.
steps.youWillDo: let the neuron try (and watch it get stuck)

steps.title: So we use more neurons
steps.body:
One straight line can't wrap a ring — it plateaus, stuck. That's not a failure; it's the reason **networks** exist.

Wire **many** neurons together and their straight lines **combine into curves**. Stack enough and they can separate almost any shape. That's the *deep* in "deep learning."

steps.title: One last time, in your words
steps.prompt: Pretend a friend asks: *"How does a neuron learn?"* Explain it the way you'd tell them.
steps.placeholder: A neuron is basically a line, and it learns by…

recall.question: Which sentence best sums up how a neuron learns?
choices: It draws a line, then nudges its dials after each mistake until it makes few mistakes
It memorizes the answer to every example
It waits for a human to set the perfect line
It guesses once and never changes
recall.explain: That's it — a line, plus the nudge-after-mistakes loop. You now understand the core of every neural network.

steps.youWillDo: explain a neuron in your own words

steps.title: What you built today 🎉
steps.body:
You sorted pets, drew a boundary, turned a neuron's dials, watched its mistakes fall, trained one from scratch, proved it really learned, and found the exact spot where one neuron needs help.

That's the real foundation of AI — the same idea runs the chatbots and image apps you've heard of, just with billions of dials.

**Next up:** see this idea make *words* — train a tiny language model in **How AI writes**.
